newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Court's coalition seen as easy winner in W.A. election.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Court's coalition seen as easy winner in W.A. election.

text.p: On the eve of Western Australia's first early election since 1943, the Liberal/National Party coalition government led by Richard Court is favoured to win comfortably by opinion polls and political pundits.
The main question marks appeared to be the winning margin and whether the 103-year conservative reign in the State's upper house, the Legislative Council, will finally be broken.
Curtin University associate professor of politics, Professor David Black, told Reuters that the Australian Labor Party knew all along it could not win the election.
"Everybody knew the reason Geoff Gallop became leader (on October 8) was to keep Labor's representation as close to last time as possible," Black said.
"Some Labor people are still expecting to lose possibly two to five seats although they might pick up one or two as well."
During the four-week long election campaign the Government ran heavily on its economic record while the Opposition highlighted longer hospital waiting lists, dirty schools and crime in the suburbs.

The Government also disputed it was the pre-election favourite, claiming mid-term electoral boundary changes had placed its fate in the hands of as few as 1800 voters in six key lower house (Legislative Assembly) seats.

Earlier this week Labor attacked the Australian Democrats decision to direct preferences to the Liberal Party in seven Assembly seats, including all six of the key seats identified by the Government as crucial to the final result.
The Democrats replied by saying it also directed preferences to Labor in seven other Assembly seats and in the Legislative Council.
Black said there is general agreement that Labor's new leader had done "a reasonable job except for losing his cool in a radio interview early in the campaign".
"Richard Court has done nothing better or worse than people would have expected," Black said. "He made no major mistakes but he was able to hold his approval ratings."
Court is the son of a former Liberal premier, Sir Charles Court.

He entered Parliament in 1982 after winning his father's old blue-ribbon conservative seat of Nedlands. He was promoted to the Liberal's frontbench two years later and deputy leader in 1987. In 1990 he opted for the backbench after a failed attempt for the top job but finally became leader in 1992.

A year later he was voted in as Premier after Labor experienced a backlash against "WA Inc", the nickname given to a string of controversial business and investment decisions by the Burke and Dowding Labor governments.
